senses: Without sense; absurd.
ety: From nonsense + -ical.

senses: Having a crocket.
ety: From crocket + -ed.
examples: For Woolworth, Gilbert designed a house that was similar, but lacier at the roof line, with intricate copper roof cresting and crocketed chimneys, and elaborately decorated dormers.

senses: Involving minor adjustments.
Showing signs of methamphetamine intoxication or involvement, or otherwise related to methamphetamine or similar drugs.
ety: From tweak + -y.
examples: As with most hacker tools, however, iPodWizard is a bit of a tweaky program, which means it's not for the faint of heart or for those utterly devoid of technical skills.
I don't need no tweaky twink / Making meth under his sink / Don't you think it's time for bed?

senses: An insurer; an underwriter.
One who takes out insurance.
A person who or thing which assures.
ety: From assure + -er.

senses: A municipal officer in the North American Dutch colonies.
ety: Borrowed from Dutch schout.

senses: A metabolite of nicotine that may improve mental ability
ety: Anagram of nicotine.

senses: especially, Plectranthus scutellarioides, also known as Coleus scutellarioides and Coleus blumei.
ety: From the genus name translingual Coleus, from Latin coleus, from Ancient Greek κολεός (koleós, “sheath”) in reference to the manner in which the stamens are united.

senses: A pinewood, pinetum, forest or grove where pine trees are grown.
ety: From pine + -ery.

senses: One of the quills of a spinet.
A barrier dividing the Ancient Roman hippodrome longitudinally.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from Latin spīna (“a thorn; a prickle, spine”). Doublet of spine.

senses: A short match, made of wood or wax.
ety: Named after Vesta, the Roman goddess of fire and the hearth.

senses: A straight section of a racetrack.
ety: From straight + way.

senses: Terrace, patio.
A representation of the ground, serving as the base for another object; a terrace.
ety: From French terrasse (“terrace”). Doublet of terrace.

senses: Covered with lint.
ety: From lint + -y.

senses: A great outcry or vociferation; loud and continued shouting or exclamation.
Any loud and continued noise.
A continued public expression, often of dissatisfaction or discontent; a popular outcry.
ety: Recorded in English since c. 1385, as Middle English clamour, from Old French clamor (modern clameur), from Latin clāmor (“a shout, cry”), from clāmō (“cry out, complain”). The verb sense "to silence" may have a distinct (unknown) etymology.

senses: Having a weir.
ety: From weir + -ed.
examples: White shrimp emigrated significantly sooner from the unweired pond than from the weired pond in most experiments, but whether the weir actually delayed emigration was unclear.

senses: Evil man; devil.
ety: From hell + man.
examples: There's this great pause as the hellmen realise they are locked in with me, the dog and the girl upstairs. There's always a few seconds while these ugly bastards stare at the bars.

senses: A coin of usually gold issued by Muslim dynasties in the Middle East, Central Asia, and South Asia, worth in India two mohurs.
ety: From Arabic أَشْرَفِيّ (ʔašrafiyy) and various descendant languages.

senses: A tropical American evergreen shrub, Bixa orellana; the lipstick tree.
The seed of this tree used as a colouring or in Latin American cooking.
An orange-red dye obtained from this seed.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish achiote, from Classical Nahuatl āchiyōtl.

senses: A district, a prefecture, particularly (historical) a second-level administrative division of the Ottoman Empire.
ety: From Ottoman Turkish سنجاق (sancâk, “subdivision of a vilayet”, literally “flag, banner”), from Proto-Turkic *sančgak (“lance, streamer attached to a spear”).

senses: A good character in a story, often a hero.
ety: From good + -ie (nominal suffix).
examples: All the press, the people and their elected leaders want to know who are the goodies and who are the baddies.
What really gets to me in these goodies versus baddies movies is just how useless the baddies are.

senses: A bet that is won only if the desired total is rolled as a pair of two of the same value, e.g. 6 from 3 and 3 rather than 4 and 2.
ety: From hard + way, i.e. the difficult way to achieve something.

senses: A mate; a boon companion.
ety: From Middle French matelot (“sailor”). Compare Dutch matroos and German Matrose. Doublet of matross.

senses: Inclined downward from opposite directions, so as to meet in a common point or line.
ety: From syn- + -clinal.
examples: The doctor's eyebrows had gone synclinal from puzzlement without his awareness.

senses: Synonym of volleyball player.
ety: From volleyball + -er.

senses: A Levantine Arab dip made of chickpea paste with various additions, such as olive oil, fresh garlic, lemon juice, and tahini, often eaten with pitta bread, or as a meze.
ety: Borrowed from Arabic حُمُّص (ḥummuṣ)., an alternative pronunciation of Arabic حِمَّص (ḥimmaṣ).

senses: a popular assembly in medieval Slavic countries.
ety: From Old East Slavic вѣче (věče, “council”) or modern Russian ве́че (véče)

senses: An Ancient Greek letter representing /k/, Ϙ / ϙ, replaced by kappa by the Classical Greek period.
The Greek numeral Ϟ (lowercase ϟ), descended from the ancient letter and having the numerical value of 90.
The archaic Cyrillic numeral Ҁ (lowercase ҁ), descended from the ancient Greek letter and having the numerical value of 90.
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek κόππα (kóppa), originally ϙόππα (qóppa).

senses: Without a cap (headgear).
Without a cap (other senses).
ety: From cap + -less. Piecewise doublet of capeless and chapeless.

senses: Having the character of film noir.
ety: From noir + -ish.
examples: His feature directing career began with the third installment of the "Alien" franchise, and before "Benjamin Button" all his movies were noirish thrillers of a sort.

senses: A malevolent and violent cannibal spirit found in Anishinaabe, Ojibwe, and Cree mythology, which is said to inhabit the body of a living person and possess him or her to commit murder.
Synonym of splake (“kind of hybrid fish”).
ety: Borrowed from Ojibwe wiindigoo, from Proto-Algonquian *wi·nteko·wa (“owl; malevolent spirit, cannibalistic monster”). Compare Plains Cree wîhtikow, ᐃᐧᐦᑎᑯᐤ (“greedy person; cannibal; giant man-eating monster”).

senses: chrism; myrrh
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μῠ́ρον (mŭ́ron).

senses: An absolute skeptic; a person who believes in the truth of nothing.
ety: From Latin nihil (“nothing”) + -ist.

senses: The homeostatic regulation of osmotic pressure in the body in order to maintain a certain water content (concentration of electrolytes, pH, etc).
ety: From osmo- + regulation.

senses: A form of croquet using short-handled mallets, and played on a hard surface.
ety: Coined 1899 by removing the first and last letters from croquet.

senses: Wasting away, declining.
ety: From tabes + -id, from Latin tābidus (“melting or wasting away, dissolving, decaying, rotting”), from tābeō + -idus.

senses: An early two-wheeled conveyance upon which one rode astride a wooden frame propelled by means of pushing the feet against the ground.
any wheeled vehicle powered by pedaling and steered with a handlebar, including but not limited to bicycles and tricycles.
ety: Borrowed from French vélocipède, from Latin velox (“swift”) + pes (“foot”).

senses: The drawing of wine from its barrel.
ety: From French tirage, from tirer (“to draw, pull”).

senses: A largemouth bass.
Anything that is unusually large.
ety: From large + -ie.
examples: The fisheries biologist also says other species seen during their surveys besides fat largies include bluegill, black crappie, redear sunfish, pumpkinseed, brown bullhead and channel catfish.
You'll want to use spinnerbaits to catch the largies, or toss topwater plugs working gaps in the vegetation.
Thick vegetation, lily pads, weed beds and any sort of cover is a typical summer home for a largie.

senses: Sharp or deadly.
Having a special power making decapitation likely.
ety: Coined by British author and scholar Lewis Carroll in the poem Jabberwocky to describe a sword, likely modeled after warp and vortex + -al.

senses: A person who drives a chariot.
ety: Inherited from Middle English charioter, from Old French charioteur (“charioteer”) and charretier (“coachman”). By surface analysis, chariot + -eer.
